summary: Defines a set of provisioning classes and textual conventions common to all clients that provision policy through the COPS protocol for Provisioning. It builds on the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: Different policy forms need some of the same boxes and labels. This document supplies those shared parts so every form can use them. It is historic now.

questions: what is the framework policy information base
what is a role in policy provisioning
how does role combination matching work
subtitle: Shared building blocks for all policy provisioning information bases.

tldr.problem: Multiple policy provisioning modules (for QoS, VPN, security) needed to share common concepts and structure. Each would duplicate definitions for roles, interfaces, and capabilities if no shared framework existed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3318 defines the Framework PIB: common provisioning classes for roles (abstract interface labels), interface role combinations, device capabilities, and basic classifier and marker elements. All policy PIBs build on these shared foundations.
tldr.outcome: This framework enabled standardized policy provisioning via COPS protocol for diverse policy domains. It is now Historic as policy provisioning and related standards have evolved.

facts.label: Core concept
facts.value: Roles and role combinations for interface-independent policy binding

today: RFC 3318 is Historic. It provided a framework for standardized policy provisioning via COPS, but policy provisioning architectures and network management approaches have evolved beyond this model.

sections.title: Shared Policy Provisioning Infrastructure
sections.content:
Network policy provisioning involves sending configuration to network devices to control their behavior. The COPS protocol (Common Open Policy Service) supports policy provisioning via multiple client types, each for a different policy domain: QoS policies (how to prioritize traffic), security policies (access control), virtual private network (VPN) policies, and others.

RFC 3318 defines the Framework PIB, a set of provisioning classes common to all policy domains. This prevents duplication and ensures consistent concepts like roles, interfaces, and capabilities across all policy types.
sections.eli5: Imagine a company where HR sets salary rules, IT sets computer rules, and Finance sets expense rules. They all need to say 'this rule applies to this department' and 'this rule applies to this branch office.' Instead of each department inventing its own way to say that, they share a common language.

sections.title: Roles and Interface Abstraction
sections.content:
The framework uses the concept of Roles to bind policies to interfaces without naming them explicitly. A role is a string label (such as 'finance', 'branch-office', 'high-priority') associated with an interface. Each interface may have multiple roles.

Provisioning classes have a RoleCombination attribute specifying which roles an interface must have for the policy to apply. For example, a policy with role combination 'finance+manager' applies only to interfaces with both the finance and manager roles. The wildcard '*' can match zero or more additional roles, allowing one policy to apply to multiple role combinations without duplication.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying 'apply this rule to interface 5, interface 7, and interface 12', you say 'apply this rule to any interface labeled finance.' If an interface is later labeled finance, it automatically gets the rule without the policy server knowing about it.

sections.title: Reporting Device Capabilities
sections.content:
When a device connects to a policy server via COPS, it sends a full state request reporting all interfaces, their role combinations, and capability sets supported. The framework defines capability classes that allow the device to declare what policy features it can implement.

Capability tables describe: what classification criteria the device supports (what packet fields it can examine), what actions it can perform, what scheduling methods it supports, what queue depths are available, and any other limitations. The policy server (PDP) uses this information to assign appropriate policies that the device can actually execute.
sections.eli5: It's like a restaurant telling a supplier 'we can make dishes with these ingredients, we have 4 cooking methods, and our oven fits this size.' The supplier then sends recipes that fit what the restaurant can actually cook.

sections.title: Installing and Updating Policies
sections.content:
The Framework PIB defines the process for policy installation. When role combinations on an interface change (e.g., an interface gains a new role), the device sends updated requests to the policy server, which responds with policies for the new role combinations.

The framework supports both full state updates (replacing all policies at once) and incremental updates (adding, modifying, or removing specific policies). This allows the policy server to send only the changes needed rather than the entire policy set.
sections.eli5: When a department gets a new rule, instead of replacing all rules everywhere, the policy server sends just the new rule. Or if a manager changes departments, the server can update just that manager's role and send any new rules that apply.

sections.title: Base Classes and Extensible Framework
sections.content:
The Framework PIB defines base provisioning classes (PRCs) that other PIBs extend. These include generic Classifier and Marker classes that can be specialized for different policy domains. It also defines textual conventions for common types (roles, OBJECT IDENTITYs, Prids) that enable consistent syntax across all PIB modules.

The framework uses indirection via Prids (provisioning instance identifiers) to allow one provisioning class to reference another, enabling reuse of parameter classes and flexible policy composition.
sections.eli5: The framework provides templates like 'here's how a classifier should look' and 'here's how a marker should work.' Other policy types (QoS, security, VPN) fill in the details for their own needs.

sections.title: Scope and Standardization
sections.content:
RFC 3318 is Informational, and its status is now Historic. It served as the foundation for standardized policy provisioning (RFC 3317 for DiffServ QoS, and other modules for other domains). The framework enabled the COPS protocol to provision diverse policy types in a uniform way.

While this specific framework has faded with changes in network policy architectures, it remains historically significant as a unified approach to policy provisioning that influenced later policy management systems.
sections.eli5: This RFC built the LEGO system. The bricks are in place, and other RFCs (like the QoS one) describe how to build with them. Eventually, people preferred different building systems, but this one worked well for many years.
